title: The architecture of a system the UK left
subtitle: Treaties, institutions and the sources of EU law
objectives: Trace the treaty framework from Rome (1957) through Maastricht (1992) to Lisbon (2009), and state the TEU/TFEU split
Distinguish regulations, directives and decisions as sources of EU secondary law under TFEU arts 288–289
Identify the roles of the Commission, the Council, the Parliament and the CJEU within the EU's institutional architecture

leadingAuthorities.role: The constitutional skeleton of the Union: values, institutions, common foreign and security policy
Defines the EU's secondary legislative instruments — regulations, directives, decisions — and the ordinary legislative procedure

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This module sits apart from the rest of your syllabus: you're learning the architecture of a legal order the UK is no longer part of. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can name the institutions — this lesson checks whether you know what each one actually does.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below is weighted towards scenario-based questions: expect 'which institution did this' rather than 'name the institution'.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the treaty chronology and the TEU/TFEU split are the scaffolding the rest of this lesson, and Lesson 2, hang off.

overview.hook: Picture an org chart for a country that doesn't quite exist — a Commission that isn't a government, a Court with no police force of its own, a Parliament that shares its lawmaking pen with a Council of national ministers. That's the European Union: an institutional design built to solve a problem no state has faced before, made up of states that keep their own sovereignty while pooling some of it. The UK spent 47 years inside this structure and shaped parts of it. This lesson is the map of how it works — read as history and comparative law, not as a system currently governing you.
overview.lawStatedNotice: The United Kingdom left the European Union on 31 January 2020 and is no longer bound by EU treaties, institutions or ongoing CJEU jurisdiction. This lesson teaches the EU's treaty framework and institutional architecture as historical and comparative grounding — material that shaped decades of UK law and remains useful for understanding retained/assimilated law and the UK's continuing relationship with the EU under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement — not as a system that currently binds UK courts or citizens. Law stated as at 1 September 2026.

parts.heading: Three treaties, one project
parts.voice: structural — a chronology students will return to as a reference
body: The European Union did not appear fully formed. It grew through three constitutional moments, each expanding what the project could do and how it was governed.

The Treaty of Rome (1957) created the European Economic Community — six founding states pooling sovereignty over a common market in goods, initially framed almost entirely in economic terms. The Treaty of Maastricht (1992) was the decisive expansion: it created the European Union itself, layered on top of the Community, added EU citizenship, and organised the whole project into three 'pillars' — the Community pillar (largely supranational) sitting alongside intergovernmental cooperation on foreign policy and justice/home affairs.

The Treaty of Lisbon (2009) is the version of the EU's constitution still in force. It abolished the three-pillar structure, merged everything into a single legal personality for the Union, and split the founding treaties into the two documents you need to know by name: the Treaty on European Union (TEU) and the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).

components.definition: The treaty currently governing the EU's constitutional structure. It ended the three-pillar system created at Maastricht, gave the Union a single legal personality, and restructured the founding treaties into the TEU and the TFEU.

interaction.prompt: Put these treaty milestones in chronological order.
items: Treaty of Rome creates the European Economic Community
Treaty of Maastricht creates the European Union and its three-pillar structure
Treaty of Lisbon abolishes the pillars and creates the TEU/TFEU split
The United Kingdom formally leaves the European Union
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the arc: 1957 economic community, 1992 political union with pillars, 2009 single legal personality under TEU/TFEU, 2020 UK exit. Everything else in this module sits inside that timeline.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the dates again — Rome (1957) is the economic starting point, Maastricht (1992) is where 'European Union' as a name and the pillar structure first appear, and Lisbon (2009) is the constitutional settlement still in force today, well before the UK's 2020 exit.

parts.heading: TEU and TFEU: a constitution in two parts
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, building the framework the rest of the module assumes
body: Since Lisbon, EU primary law lives in two treaties that operate as a single constitutional document but do different jobs. Getting this split right matters because exam questions and academic commentary routinely cite 'article X TEU' or 'article Y TFEU' and expect you to know, roughly, which kind of provision that signals.

The Treaty on European Union (TEU) is the skeleton: it sets out the Union's founding values, its institutions in outline, the accession and withdrawal procedures (this is where Article 50, the withdrawal clause the UK triggered, lives), and the framework for the Common Foreign and Security Policy.

The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) is the detail: the substantive policy areas — the internal market, free movement, competition law, agriculture — the institutions' powers and procedures in depth, and the legal instruments through which the EU actually legislates. If the TEU tells you an institution exists, the TFEU tells you what it can do.

components.label: TEU vs TFEU at a glance
points: TEU — constitutional skeleton: values, institutions in outline, enlargement and withdrawal (Article 50), foreign and security policy
TFEU — operational detail: substantive policy areas, institutional powers and procedures, the legislative instruments (Articles 288–289)
Both treaties have equal legal status — neither is 'senior' to the other; they are read together as a single body of primary law

interaction.prompt: Which treaty contains Article 50 — the withdrawal procedure the UK used to leave the EU?
options: The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — Article 50 sits in the TEU, alongside the other 'constitutional' provisions on membership, values and institutions in outline.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Article 50 is a TEU provision — it governs membership itself (accession and withdrawal), which is constitutional-skeleton material, not the operational detail found in the TFEU.

parts.heading: Regulations, directives, decisions: the EU's own hierarchy of instruments
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: TFEU Article 288 is the single most important provision for understanding how EU law actually reached the ground in member states, because it defines the instruments the institutions use to legislate — and each one behaves completely differently once made.

A regulation is 'general application' and 'binding in its entirety' and 'directly applicable in all Member States' — it becomes law automatically, with no national implementing step required, the moment it enters into force. A directive is 'binding, as to the result to be achieved,' on the states it's addressed to, but leaves 'the choice of form and methods' to national authorities — meaning member states had to pass their own domestic legislation to transpose it, usually within a set deadline. A decision is 'binding in its entirety' but only on those to whom it is addressed — it can target a single state, company or individual, and doesn't set general rules at all.

Article 289 then supplies the procedure: most legislation is made under the 'ordinary legislative procedure', which requires the Council (representing member state governments) and the European Parliament (directly elected) to agree the same text — a co-decision model that gives both an intergovernmental and a democratic check on new EU law.

components.text: A regulation shall have general application. It shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States. A directive shall be binding, as to the result to be achieved, upon each Member State to which it is addressed, but shall leave to the national authorities the choice of form and methods. A decision shall be binding in its entirety. A decision which specifies those to whom it is addressed shall be binding only on them.
elements: Regulation — general, binding, directly applicable, no transposition needed
Directive — binding as to result only, form/method left to the member state, requires transposition
Decision — binding in full, but only on its specified addressees

interaction.prompt: Under Article 288 TFEU, which instrument requires a member state to pass its own domestic legislation before it takes effect nationally?
options: A decision addressed to that state
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A directive binds as to the result but deliberately leaves the mechanics to national authorities — that's the transposition step that regulations skip entirely.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at the wording each instrument gets in Article 288. Only the directive is described as leaving 'the choice of form and methods' to national authorities — that's the language that signals a domestic transposition step is needed.

parts.heading: Who does what: the four-institution map
parts.voice: institutional — a 'who does what' briefing, not a narrative
body: Four institutions do most of the work, and confusing their roles is the single most common mistake students make in this area. Each has a genuinely distinct job.

The European Commission proposes legislation, administers EU policy day to day, and enforces EU law against member states — it can bring infringement proceedings against a state that fails to comply. The Council of the European Union represents the governments of the member states, ministers by policy area, and co-legislates alongside Parliament under the ordinary legislative procedure. The European Parliament is the only directly elected institution, representing EU citizens rather than states, and shares the legislative pen with the Council.

The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) interprets EU law and ensures it is applied consistently across all member states — it hears direct actions, and, critically, answers preliminary references sent up by national courts asking what a piece of EU law means. It is not itself a legislature, and it has no police force of its own: enforcement of its judgments still runs through national institutions and the Commission's infringement powers.

components.label: The four-institution map
points: Commission — proposes law, administers policy, enforces EU law against member states
Council — represents national governments; co-legislates with Parliament
Parliament — directly elected by EU citizens; co-legislates with the Council
CJEU — interprets EU law, ensures consistent application, answers preliminary references from national courts

interaction.prompt: A member state fails to transpose a directive by its deadline. Tap the fact that identifies which institution is best placed to act first.
interaction.scenarioText: Six months after the transposition deadline passes, the Commission opens infringement proceedings against the state. The Council notes the delay at a later ministerial meeting. The Parliament debates the issue in a committee session the following year.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Enforcement against a non-complying member state is the Commission's job — it's the institution with the power to bring infringement proceedings, not the Council or Parliament.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the enforcement action, not the discussion. Only the Commission has the power to open infringement proceedings against a state; the Council and Parliament's roles here are legislative and deliberative, not enforcement.

parts.heading: Why learn the architecture of a system you've left
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by justifying its own place in the syllabus
body: It's fair to ask why an LLB studying UK law needs a working knowledge of the Commission's enforcement powers or the difference between a regulation and a directive. Three reasons, and they'll recur across this module.

First, comparative grounding: understanding a supranational legal order with direct effect and primacy over national law sharpens your sense of what makes the UK's own dualist, parliamentary-sovereignty system distinctive — Public law's sovereignty lessons make far more sense once you've seen the alternative model up close. Second, historical fact: EU law shaped UK statute and common law for 47 years, and a huge body of 'retained' — now 'assimilated' — EU law still sits in the UK statute book, interpreted using EU-law concepts even though the EU institutions no longer have jurisdiction over it. Third, currency: the UK–EU relationship remains active under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, and understanding how the EU actually functions is necessary to understand what that relationship still involves.

None of this makes current CJEU case law binding on a UK court today. Keep that distinction sharp as you go into Lesson 2, which is about a doctrine — supremacy — that the UK absorbed for decades and then, by leaving, deliberately stepped outside of.

components.definition: The body of former EU law retained in UK domestic statute after Brexit, now governed by UK statute rather than EU treaties — a preview of a concept this module returns to in later lessons on the domestication of EU law.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a ruling handed down by the CJEU today automatically binds a UK court?
interaction.explanation: Not binding. Since exit, UK courts are not bound by ongoing CJEU jurisprudence. Older, pre-exit CJEU case law has a specific — and limited — retained status under domestic statute, and even that is a matter of UK law, not EU authority; new CJEU rulings carry no automatic force in UK courts at all.

testPool.prompt: Name the two treaties that, since Lisbon, together make up EU primary law.
acceptableAnswers: Treaty on European Union and Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
testPool.modelAnswer: The Treaty on European Union (TEU) and the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).

testPool.prompt: Which treaty first created the European Union and its three-pillar structure?
Which of the following is NOT one of the EU's binding secondary legislative instruments under Article 288 TFEU?
testPool.trapExplanation: Article 288 does list recommendations and opinions, but explicitly states they 'shall have no binding force' — they're persuasive, not legal instruments in the same sense as regulations, directives and decisions.

items: Treaty of Rome establishes the EEC
Treaty of Maastricht creates the EU
Treaty of Lisbon creates the TEU/TFEU split

testPool.prompt: Under Article 288 TFEU, what makes a regulation different from a decision, even though both are described as 'binding in their entirety'?
options: A regulation has general application; a decision (where it names addressees) binds only those specified
A regulation is optional; a decision is compulsory
A regulation only applies to one member state at a time

testPool.prompt: In the extract from Article 288 TFEU below, highlight the phrase that most precisely explains why directives require domestic transposition.
testPool.passage: A directive shall be binding, as to the result to be achieved, upon each Member State to which it is addressed, but shall leave to the national authorities the choice of form and methods.
testPool.ratioSentence: but shall leave to the national authorities the choice of form and methods

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that shows this instrument is a regulation rather than a directive.
testPool.scenarioText: A new EU food-labelling rule enters into force on 1 January and is immediately enforceable in every member state's courts with no national legislation passed to implement it. Businesses must comply from that date.
tappableSpans: with no national legislation passed to implement it
testPool.correctSpan: with no national legislation passed to implement it
testPool.explanation: Direct applicability with no transposition step is the defining feature of a regulation under Article 288 — a directive would have required a national implementing measure first.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario describes a decision, rather than a directive, under Article 288 TFEU?
testPool.scenarioA: The Commission issues a ruling addressed specifically to one named company, ordering it to repay unlawful state aid, binding only on that company.
testPool.scenarioB: The Union sets a target for reducing packaging waste 'to be achieved' by all member states, leaving each state to choose its own implementing method and deadline.
testPool.explanation: A is a decision: binding in full, but only on its named addressee. B is a directive — binding as to the result, with the form and method left to national authorities.

testPool.prompt: A national government misses the transposition deadline for an EU directive by eight months. Under the institutional map in this lesson, which institution has the power to bring infringement proceedings against it?
testPool.explanation: Enforcement of EU law against a non-complying member state is a Commission function — it can open infringement proceedings, which may ultimately lead to a referral to the CJEU.

testPool.prompt: Which institution is the only one of the four directly elected by EU citizens?
options: The Council of the European Union

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that the TEU and TFEU have equal legal status, with neither treaty 'senior' to the other?
sliderLabels: Not confident — one outranks the other
Confident — they are equal in status
testPool.explanation: Correct: since Lisbon, the TEU and TFEU are treated as a single body of primary law of equal legal status, despite their different focus (constitutional skeleton vs operational detail).

testPool.prompt: An EU regulation on data-transfer standards enters into force. A member state's parliament debates whether it needs to pass an implementing statute before the regulation can be relied on in its national courts. Analyse whether that step is necessary.
factsToOrder: The instrument is described as a 'regulation'
It has entered into force at EU level
The member state's parliament is debating whether an implementing statute is required

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a national implementing statute is required before an EU regulation can be relied on in national courts.
modelAnswer.rule: Article 288 TFEU provides that a regulation has general application, is binding in its entirety, and is directly applicable in all member states — no national implementing measure is contemplated or required.
modelAnswer.application: Because the instrument in question is a regulation (not a directive), it takes effect automatically across the Union from the point it enters into force. The national parliament's debate about an implementing statute rests on a category error — that step is required for directives, not regulations.
modelAnswer.conclusion: No implementing statute is necessary; the regulation is directly applicable and enforceable in national courts without one.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best describes the ordinary legislative procedure under Article 289 TFEU?
options: The Commission alone enacts legislation without further approval
The Council and the European Parliament must agree the same legislative text
The CJEU approves legislation before it can take effect
testPool.trapExplanation: The Commission proposes legislation but does not enact it alone, and the CJEU has no role in the legislative procedure itself — its job is interpretation and adjudication, not approval of legislation. The ordinary legislative procedure is a co-decision model between Council and Parliament.

testPool.prompt: Name the four institutions covered in this lesson's institutional map.
acceptableAnswers: the Commission, the Council, the European Parliament and the Court of Justice of the European Union
testPool.modelAnswer: The European Commission, the Council of the European Union, the European Parliament, and the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU).

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating the EU's institutions as interchangeable — assuming any of the four could propose, enforce or adjudicate. Each has one job; scenario questions are testing whether you can spot which one applies.
